why: You choose k '(' and k ')' and match each '(' with a later ')'; the score is the sum of (close index - open index), which equals sum of chosen close indices minus sum of chosen open indices. So greedily take the k leftmost '(' and the k rightmost ')', for the best feasible k; the number of feasible pairs is bounded by the stack-style greedy matching count.
hints: The score of a set of pairs only depends on which indices you chose, not on how you pair them. Why?
Total score = (sum of chosen ')' indices) - (sum of chosen '(' indices). For a fixed k that is maximised by the k earliest '(' and the k latest ')', as long as k pairs can be matched at all.

Count the maximum matchable pairs K with a counter (like a stack of open brackets). Then for k = 1..K add opens[k-1] and closes[-k] to running sums and keep the best difference; each extra pair adds less than the previous, so you can stop once it stops helping. O(n).
pitfalls: You do not have to use every bracket: in "()()" the best is the single outer pair (0, 3) with score 3.
A ')' must come after the '(' it is paired with; a string like ")(" scores 0.
Pairs are counted by index difference, so nested pairs (0, 3) and (1, 2) give 3 + 1 = 4.
statement:
You are given a string s of the characters ( and ). Choose some pairs of positions (i, j) with i < j, s[i] = '(' and s[j] = ')', using each position in at most one pair. The chosen characters then form a balanced selection: as many opening as closing parentheses. The score of a pair is j - i, and the score of the selection is the sum over its pairs. Return the maximum possible score (0 if no pair can be formed).

Worked example 1: s = "(())"

  • Opens at 0 and 1, closes at 2 and 3.
  • Pair (0, 3) and (1, 2): 3 + 1 = 4. Pairing (0, 2) and (1, 3) also gives 2 + 2 = 4.

Answer: 4.

Worked example 2: s = "()()"

  • Using both pairs (0, 1) and (2, 3) gives 1 + 1 = 2.
  • Using only the outer pair (0, 3) gives 3; the middle characters are left out.
  • (1, 2) is not allowed because s[1] is ')'.

Answer: 3.
constraints:
• 1 <= s.length <= 10^5 (not stated in the source; a reasonable bound)
  • s contains only '(' and ')'.
